stem: A team building a documentation-generation agent notices their loop occasionally stops after a tool_use turn without executing the tool, because their code has an early-return bug that skips the tool-execution branch under a rare condition. The next request sent to the model omits the corresponding tool_result. What happens, and what does this reveal about a subtle loop-implementation requirement?
explanation: Sending a follow-up request with a dangling tool_use block and no matching tool_result is malformed and will typically error or produce broken behavior — this reveals that every tool_use the model emits must be paired with a corresponding tool_result before the next request is sent, a requirement beyond simply checking stop_reason correctly.

choices.text: Skipping execution leaves a tool_use with no matching tool_result, making the next request malformed
choices.reasoning: Correct: this identifies a real, subtle loop-implementation requirement beyond stop_reason handling — the conversation structure requires every tool_use block to be matched with a tool_result before continuing.

choices.text: Nothing unusual happens; the model automatically supplies a placeholder tool_result on the next turn
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the model doesn't fabricate a tool_result for a skipped execution — the application is responsible for supplying one, and omitting it produces a malformed request.

choices.text: This is only a problem if the tool in question has destructiveHint set to true
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the tool_use/tool_result pairing requirement applies to the conversation structure generally, regardless of any particular tool's annotation hints.

choices.text: This only matters when using the Batch API, not real-time requests
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the requirement to pair tool_use with tool_result applies to the conversation structure generally, not specifically to Batch requests.

choices.text: This reveals that stop_reason should be checked twice per turn instead of once
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: checking stop_reason twice doesn't address the actual issue — a missing tool_result for an already-emitted tool_use block, which is a structural completeness requirement, not a stop_reason-checking frequency issue.

choices.text: This reveals that the model silently ignores any tool_use block that isn't followed by a tool_result
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: rather than silently ignoring it, an unpaired tool_use typically causes a malformed-request error on the next call, which is exactly why the pairing matters.

stem: A coordinator spawns four parallel subagents to check four different data sources for the same fact, expecting to synthesize whichever answers come back. One subagent's tool crashes with an unhandled exception rather than returning any structured result at all — not even a shaped failure object. What architectural gap does this expose?
explanation: This exposes a gap in defensive subagent design — the coordinator's synthesis logic needs to handle the case where a subagent doesn't return anything usable at all (a crash, not just a structured failure), e.g. via a timeout/catch at the coordinator level, since even well-designed structured-failure conventions only help if the subagent actually gets to return something.

choices.text: The coordinator needs its own timeout/catch to handle a subagent crashing with no output at all
choices.reasoning: Correct: structured failure conventions only work if the subagent gets a chance to return something — a genuine crash with no output requires the coordinator to have its own defensive handling (timeout, catch) as a complementary safeguard.

choices.text: There's no gap; a crashed subagent is functionally identical to one returning a structured failure result
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a crash producing no output at all is a different failure mode than a subagent successfully returning a structured failure object — the coordinator needs to handle both, and a crash specifically requires its own defensive handling.

choices.text: The fix is to ensure only one subagent is ever spawned at a time, never in parallel
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this abandons the benefit of parallel subagents for independent workstreams and doesn't address the actual gap — handling a subagent that returns nothing at all.

choices.text: The fix is to switch the crashed subagent to a higher-tier model, which never crashes
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier doesn't eliminate the possibility of a tool-level crash or unhandled exception — the coordinator still needs defensive handling for this case regardless of model tier.

choices.text: The fix is to give the crashed subagent more tools so it has alternative ways to complete its task
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: more tools doesn't address an unhandled exception crashing the subagent entirely — the actual gap is the coordinator's own defensive handling for a subagent producing no output.

choices.text: This reveals that provenance metadata should have been required on the crashed subagent's output
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: provenance concerns attaching source information to successful claims — it doesn't address the coordinator's need to handle a subagent producing no output at all due to a crash.

stem: A due-diligence system needs to review a company's public filings (a fixed, always-the-same lookup step), then based on what those filings reveal, decide which of several follow-up investigation paths to pursue (litigation history, executive backgrounds, or subsidiary structure — chosen dynamically based on red flags found). Which combination of patterns fits this two-phase shape?
explanation: This is a hybrid: prompt chaining fits the fixed, always-the-same public-filings lookup step, and dynamic decomposition (or orchestrator-workers, if the candidate follow-up paths are a bounded, known set the coordinator picks among) fits the findings-dependent second phase — recognizing that a real system can combine patterns across phases rather than forcing the whole system into one label.

choices.text: Prompt chaining for the fixed filings lookup, then dynamic decomposition for the findings-dependent phase
choices.reasoning: Correct: the first phase is a fixed, always-the-same step (prompt chaining), while the second phase's path depends on what's found (dynamic decomposition, or orchestrator-workers if the candidate paths are a bounded known set) — combining patterns by phase captures this accurately.

choices.text: Parallel subagents for the entire system, since due diligence should always investigate everything at once
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the second phase's follow-up paths depend on findings from the first phase, which contradicts the independence parallel subagents require, and running every possible investigation regardless of relevance wastes effort.

choices.text: Routing only, since there are three follow-up investigation paths to choose between
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: routing handles stable, mutually-exclusive classification, but this scenario involves choosing dynamically based on evolving findings (and potentially multiple paths applying), and it ignores the fixed first phase entirely.

choices.text: Prompt chaining for the entire system end to end, in one fixed sequence
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the second phase is explicitly findings-dependent and not a fixed, predetermined sequence, which rules out pure prompt chaining for the whole system.

choices.text: Orchestrator-workers for the entire system from the very first step, since a coordinator role exists throughout
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the first phase (public filings lookup) is a fixed, always-the-same step with nothing to dynamically decide — applying orchestrator-workers' dynamic-decision overhead there is unnecessary.

choices.text: A single subagent handling everything sequentially with no distinction between the two phases
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this discards the meaningful distinction between the fixed lookup phase and the findings-dependent investigation phase, missing the actual shape of the work.

stem: A "triage" subagent's role is purely to categorize incoming support tickets and hand them off — it never needs to search external sources, edit anything, or communicate directly with customers. It's currently given 9 tools: 3 categorization-relevant ones plus 6 unrelated ones (web search, file edit, email send, calendar access, etc.) inherited from a shared subagent template. What's the architecturally sound fix?
explanation: Prune the toolset down to roughly the 3-5 tools the triage role actually needs, removing the 6 unrelated ones inherited from a shared template — a broad, inherited toolset still causes the same tool-selection complexity and role-drift risk regardless of how the extra tools got there, matching the documented guidance to scope subagents narrowly to their actual role.

choices.text: Prune the toolset to only the categorization-relevant tools, removing the rest
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented guidance directly — a broad toolset causes role drift and selection complexity regardless of whether the extra tools came from a shared template or were added individually; the fix is scoping to the role's actual needs.

choices.text: Keep all 9 tools, since they came from a shared template and templates should never be customized per subagent
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the documented anti-pattern — a broad toolset degrades selection quality and causes role drift, regardless of whether it originated from a shared template.

choices.text: Add three more tools to round the total up to an even dozen for consistency with other subagent roles
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adding more unrelated tools compounds the role-drift risk rather than fixing it — the documented fix is narrowing to the role's actual needs.

choices.text: Remove all 9 tools, including the categorization-relevant ones, and give the subagent zero tools
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this would prevent the triage subagent from performing its actual categorization role at all — the fix is removing the unrelated tools, not the relevant ones.

choices.text: Keep the 9 tools but add a longer system prompt telling the subagent which of the 9 to prefer
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: relying on prompt-level preference guidance to compensate for an overly broad toolset doesn't resolve the underlying selection-complexity and role-drift problem — removing the unneeded tools does.

choices.text: Switch the subagent to a lower-tier model, which will naturally ignore the unrelated tools
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: lowering model capability doesn't remove the unrelated tools from the available toolset or reliably prevent their selection — the fix is pruning the toolset itself.
